title: Neuro-Ophthalmology & Optic Nerve Atlas: From Dysfunction to Treatment Protocols
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide for ophthalmologists covering optic nerve dysfunction signs, the diagnostic spectrum of disc elevation, multiple sclerosis management, and complex pupillary pathways. This poster integrates verbatim input with essential clinical differentials for resident-level mastery.

sections.title: Clinical Signs of Optic Nerve Dysfunction
content: Reduced v.a for distance and near (common but not spesiﬁc)

rows: Demylination, toxic-nutritional, leber heriditary optic neuropathy, compression
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION), glaucoma, disc drusen
Upper temporal defect (Not respecting vertical meridian)

branches: Spinal cord: Weakness, stiffness, sphincter disturbance, sensory loss
Transient: Lhermitte sign (electrical sensation on neck ﬂexion), Uhthoff phenomenon (worsening on exercise/heat)

rows: Change in optic n appearance; Lesions in the white matter of the brain
Conduction delay and reduction in amplitude

sections.title: Treatment Protocols: Multiple Sclerosis
content: Steroid Regimen: 1g methy prednisolone Na succinate daily for 3 days
Followed by: Oral prednisolone 1mg/kg daily for 11 days
Other Therapies: Interferon beta, Glatiramer acetate, Monoclonal antibodies

branches: First attack: IV corticosteroid, interferon b, glatimet
Relapsing (Active/Highly Active): Natalizumab, Ocrelizumab, Alemtuzumab, cladribine, ﬁngolimod, natalizumab, mitoxantrone

sections.title: Steroid Tapering Regimen for AION
content: Step 3: 3 days later, reduce dose to 50-60mg/4w or until symptoms resolve & ESR/CRP normalizes
Step 4: Reduce daily dose by 10mg/day every 2 weeks until 20mg/day is reached
Step 5: 2.5 mg reduction every 2-4 weeks until 10mg reached, then 1mg reduction every 1-2 months
Bone+GIT Protection: VitD, calcium, proton pump inhibitor
Vascular Prophylaxis: Aspirin 600mg then 100mg/day to reduce visual loss and stroke risk

sections.title: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) Management
sections.content: Treatment of gaint cell arteritis without AAION: Oral prednisolone 1mg/kg daily governed by symptoms, level of ESR, and CRP. CRP level is important in monitoring disease activity as it falls more rapidly than ESR in response to tratment.

branches: Pseudopapilledema (Drusen, Tilted disc, Myelinated fibers, Crowded hypermetropic disc)

sections.title: Causes of Raised Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
content: 3. Space occupying intracranial lesions including hge
4. Impairment of CSF absorbtion (meningitis, subarachnoid hges, trauma)
6. Cerebral edema from blunt head trauma
8. Hypersecretion of CSF by choroid plexus tumour (very rare)

rows: Mild Disc hyperemia + preservation of optic cup; Indistinct peripapillary retinal n striation and disc margins; Absent SVP

Normal or reduced VA; Sever disc hyperaemia; Moderate elevation, indistinct margins; Absent cup; Venous engorgement; Peripapillary ﬂame hge and cotton wool spots; Paton lines (circumferential folds); Macular fan; Enlarged blind spot
VA variable, field constricts; Disc elevation without CWS or hge; Optociliary shunts; Drusen-like crystalline deposition (corpora amylacea)
VA severely impaired; Discs grey-white slightly elevated; Few crossing blood vessels; Indistinct margins
CHARGE syndrome, Goldenhar syndrome, CNS abnormalities

sections.title: The Light Reflex Pathway
content: 5. Pretectal nucleus (Midbrain/Superior Colliculi): Nasal fibers cross, Temporal fibers stay ipsilateral
6. Edinger Westphal nuclei (both sides receive bilateral input)
8. Ciliary ganglion (via nerve to inferior oblique)
NOTE ON NEURONS: Red = 1st order (sensory), Brown = 2nd order (internuncial), Baby blue = 3rd order (preganglionic motor), Dark blue = 4th order (postganglionic motor)

rows: Both pupils dilate instead of constrict (Swinging light)

content.explanation: Asymmetrical pupil diameter implies disease of the efferent motor nerve or the iris itself. Sensory lesions (like RAPD) do NOT cause anisocoria.

sections.title: Sympathetic Pathway (Pupillary Dilation)
content: 1st Order (Central): Posterior hypothalamus descends uncrossed to Ciliospinal Center of Budge (C8-T2).
2nd Order (Preganglionic): From Center of Budge to Superior Cervical Ganglion (neck).
3rd Order (Postganglionic): Ascends along Internal Carotid Artery to Cavernous Sinus; joins V1 (trigeminal); reaches Dilator Pupillae via Nasociliary and Long Ciliary nerves.

sections.title: Neuro-Ophthalmology Red Flags
content: Sudden VA loss with headache and jaw claudication (GCA)
Electrical sensation on neck flexion (Lhermitte sign)
Pupillary dilation on swinging flashlight test (RAPD)
Absent Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP) in disc elevation
Sudden worsening of symptoms with heat/exercise (Uhthoff phenomenon)
